finding.claim: deleteAccount calls canDelete() but discards the boolean result, so no authorization is enforced. Any caller can delete any account by id. closeAccount correctly uses assertCanDelete, which throws on failure.
finding.source: Any authenticated user calling DELETE /accounts/{id} with an arbitrary account id
finding.sink: accounts.remove(id) at line 23, which deletes the account

trace.note: deleteAccount(User u, long id) is the entry point for DELETE /accounts/{id}; id is attacker-controlled
account looked up by attacker-supplied id
canDelete(u, a) returns a boolean that is ignored; no throw or early return

finding.guards_checked: canDelete at line 22 is the only check and its result is unused. assertCanDelete (which would throw) is not called here. There is no other auth layer in the repo; this is the only source file. No ownership check precedes the removal.

verdict.guard_found: canDelete (src/AccountService.java:9-11) returns a boolean, and the call at line 22 discards it. assertCanDelete, which throws, is only called in closeAccount (line 29). No other guard exists.
verdict.reason: At src/AccountService.java:22 canDelete(u, a) is a bare statement whose boolean result is ignored, so accounts.remove(id) at line 23 runs for any authenticated user. The line 9-11 check (admin or owner) is never enforced here, unlike assertCanDelete at line 29.

verdict_facts.guard_found: canDelete at src/AccountService.java:22 (returns boolean, result discarded); assertCanDelete (throws) exists but is only used in closeAccount at line 29. No other guard.
verdict_facts.reason: src/AccountService.java:22 calls canDelete (returns boolean, lines 9-11) as a bare statement, so accounts.remove(id) at line 23 runs for any authenticated user regardless of ownership or admin status.
